# DiceTable

> DiceTable is a free browser tool for comparing tabletop dice rolls by their exact probability. Build a table of named rolls, read the full distribution and summary stats for each, and overlay them on one chart to compare and balance them.

DiceTable is for tabletop and strategy gamers who want to understand and balance dice rolls without learning a scripting language or any statistics. It works with any system, because a roll is just a dice expression. Everything happens in a graphical table: there is no notation to memorize first and no math background required.

## What it computes

All probabilities are exact. DiceTable enumerates each die's distribution and combines them by full convolution, so every number is the true probability of that outcome. It does not use normal or uniform approximations, and it does not sample or simulate to produce its stats.

A roll can be scored three ways. Sum mode adds the dice into one total. Pool mode counts successes instead: each die succeeds when it meets a threshold (for example, 8 or higher on a d10), the result is the number of successes, and the flat modifier grants or removes successes directly (a result never drops below zero). Pool odds are exact too, including rerolls.

Check mode covers if-then mechanics without any scripting: the roll first tries to clear a number, then applies an effect scaled by how it went. A check row carries its check dice and modifier, the number to clear, its own effect dice and modifier, and how much of that effect lands on a success and on a failure (all of it, half rounded down, or none). Full on a success and nothing on a failure is an attack roll; half on a success and full on a failure is a save-for-half spell. A check of exactly one die can also have a critical: chosen faces that always succeed and either roll double the dice, roll one extra die, or add the highest the dice can show. Criticals are classified on the face the die shows, so advantage raises the chance of one. The row's average counts the failures, so it is the expected result per attempt rather than per success, which is the number to balance two mechanics against each other with. A check row still produces one distribution, so every chart, target, and comparison view treats it like any other roll on the totals scale.

For each roll it reports:

- Mean (the long-run average result).
- Standard deviation and variance (how spread out or consistent the results are).
- Mode (the most likely result, or results when several tie).
- Range (the smallest and largest possible results).
- Hit probability (how often the roll meets a target you set).

## Dice notation it understands

DiceTable displays standard tabletop dice notation while everything is edited with graphical controls, so there is no notation to type:

- Count and die, such as 3d8 (roll three eight-sided dice and add them).
- Flat modifier, such as +2 or -1, added to the total.
- Keep highest or lowest, such as 4d6kh3 (roll four six-sided dice, keep the highest 3) or klN.
- Keep across parts (shown as · keep highest 1): keep only the best or worst dice of the whole roll instead of adding every part, which works across dice of different sizes. 1d8 + 1d6 · keep highest 1 is the trait-and-wild-die roll. It replaces the per-part keep rules rather than stacking with them.
- Reroll one or more chosen faces, once or always (shown as reroll 1s always).
- Explode one or more chosen faces (shown as explode 6): on those faces, roll again and add, with a depth cap that keeps results readable.
- Count successes (dice pools), shown as count ≥8 or count ≤2: the roll's result is how many dice meet the threshold, and the flat modifier becomes auto-successes (+2 auto). Keep and explode apply only to summed rolls.
- Checks, shown as 1d20 + 7 ≥15 → 1d8 + 4 · crit 20 ×dice: what you roll, the number it clears, the effect that follows, and any critical rule. Non-default outcome scaling is spelled out too, as half on a success or full on a failure.

## Roll modes

A roll mode applies to the whole expression:

- Normal (roll once).
- Advantage (roll twice and take the higher result).
- Disadvantage (roll twice and take the lower result).

Roll modes affect summed rolls and check rolls. On a check row the mode applies to the check itself, never to the effect. A pool roll keeps its setting for when it switches back to summing, but counting successes ignores it.

## Comparing and balancing rolls

Rows appear in an overlay chart, each with its own color. A big table is drawn twenty rolls at a time, so the lines stay readable: the chart names the range it is showing ("Showing 21 to 40 of 75 rolls") and pages through the rest in table order, with totals and successes paging separately. Enlarging one chart on a wide screen with a mouse draws every roll at once instead, as a faint field: past about thirty rolls there are more curves than there are ways to tell one pen from another, so picking a name from the legend lights that roll up against all the others rather than asking anyone to follow a hundred lines. A phone, a touch screen, a narrow window, or both charts on screen at once all keep the paged twenty. Every roll still carries its own numbers in the table. The chart has four views:

- PMF: how likely each exact result is.
- CDF: the chance of rolling at most a given number.
- CCDF: the chance of rolling at least a given number, useful for "beat the DC" checks.
- Target: per-row hit-rate bars once you set one or more target numbers.

Summed rolls and check rolls chart together, because both produce totals; pool rolls chart on a separate panel, because counting successes means a different axis. When a check row fails often, the resulting pile of mass at zero is capped on the PMF view and labelled with its exact chance, so one row's miss rate cannot flatten every other curve.

You can set up to five targets (for example armor classes or save DCs) and choose how a roll is compared to them: at least, greater than, at most, less than, or exactly. A Hit % column then shows how often each summed roll meets each target. Pool rolls answer to a separate shared list of up to five pool targets ("at least n successes") instead, so tiered thresholds can be compared side by side. A built-in roller can also simulate any summed roll, using the same exact odds the chart shows.

A dedicated Target hit view compares every roll against all of your targets at once, three ways. A grid shows each roll's hit chance per target, color-coded from reliable to long shot and sortable by any target column. Curves plot each summed roll's hit chance for every possible target value, with your current targets marked, all of them at once by default and twenty at a time on request. Bars show one panel per target with rolls ranked by hit chance. Pool rolls appear in the grid and bars under their own columns, one per shared pool target, alongside the numeric target columns the summed rolls answer to.

Two more views answer "who wins?" directly, again with exact math rather than simulation. The Roll-off view imagines every roll rolling once and shows each roll's chance of producing the single highest result, with ties counted separately (nobody wins a tie outright). The Head-to-head view is a matrix of one-on-one odds: each cell is how often the row roll strictly beats the column roll, ignoring every other row, with the tie chance available on each cell. It draws the first twenty-four rolls of a bigger table and says so, since the lattice grows with the square of the row count; Roll-off ranks every roll at once. Pool rolls take part on their success-count scale, so cross-scale match-ups are usually lopsided.

Any row can also be pinned as a baseline. Every other row then shows how it differs instead of its own numbers: how much higher or lower it averages, whether it is swingier or steadier, and how its hit chances compare, each as a signed, color-coded delta in place of the value it replaces. Selecting a row's deltas opens a comparison panel for that row, holding a short plain-language verdict (for example "Averages 1.5 higher · swingier · hits 12% more often") and the numbers behind it laid out side by side: this roll, the baseline, and the difference. Average and spread comparisons only appear between rolls scored the same way; a roll on a different scale from the baseline keeps its own average, carries a marker that opens the same panel, and is compared by hit chance alone. A caption above the table names the pinned roll.

## Sharing a comparison

A table of rolls travels as a link, as raw JSON, or as a downloadable file. An Image button in the top bar produces a picture from any view, and the picture matches the view it came from. The Table view renders its comparison chart, with pool rolls in their own Successes panel stacked under the Totals one and grouped hit-rate bars when the chart is on the target view. Target hit renders whichever sub-view is selected: Grid as one board per scale with rolls down the side and targets across, each cell carrying the hit chance as a percentage, a proportional bar and a colour band from reliable to long shot; Bars as one panel per target with rolls ranked inside it; Curves as hit chance plotted across every candidate target value. Grid and Bars honour the All / Sum / Pools filter and the grid's column sort, while Curves always plots the sum rolls, so the picture matches the controls that are set. Roll-off renders the win bars in whichever order its sort chip is on. Head-to-head renders the pairwise matrix. Every card takes an optional title and states on itself whatever it left out, such as rolls too complex to compute, rolls with no dice yet, or rolls past a card's row limit. Copying it puts the picture and the share link on the clipboard together, so pasting into a chat gives the image and pasting into a text field gives the URL. The picture is drawn from the computed distributions rather than screenshotted, and on a phone it can go through the system share sheet.

## Privacy

DiceTable runs entirely in your browser. Your rolls and settings are stored on your own device, and the site collects only anonymous page analytics, anonymous performance metrics, and anonymous crash reports. There are no accounts. A table of rolls can be shared as a link or exported as a JSON file and imported back; share-link data travels in the URL fragment and is never sent to a server.
